title: First, life
hookLine: asked about death, Confucius: not yet knowing life, how can we know death?

cards: A student asks his teacher the big one. The student is Zilu, one of his disciples. The teacher is Confucius.
First Zilu asks how to serve the spirits of the dead. Confucius answers with a question: if you can't yet serve the living, how could you serve the spirits? Zilu doesn't let go.
All right, he says. Then may I ask about death? And the answer, in the Analects, comes back short: not yet knowing life, how can you know death?

teach.b: It can sound like a dodge. A student asks about death and gets a question back. Some readers do hear it that way: a teacher steering away from what he doesn't claim to know.
But listen to both answers. Serve the living, then think of serving the spirits.
Know life, then ask about death. Neither says the question is foolish. Both say there's an order, and you're not at the end of it yet.
And Confucius cared about the dead. The Analects speak with care about funerals and about remembering parents after they're gone.
One saying in the first book, from his disciple Zengzi, asks for care in the rites when parents die, and for remembering them long after. So the order isn't the living instead of the dead.
The way you treat the living is where you learn to honor anyone at all. Zilu wanted the answer to the biggest question.
Confucius handed him a smaller, harder job: the life in front of you, the people in front of you, today.
If death is a door no one can see through, there's still a whole house on this side of it, and the rooms need tending.
Some hear that as wisdom, some as a sidestep. Either way, it sends you back to the kitchen table instead of the stars.

how: The Analects are read and studied by Confucian teachers, students and families; this exchange with Zilu is a passage readers turn to when they ask what Confucius taught about death.

o: the opening rite performed at a Chinese funeral
a race to finish your work before anyone else does
Confucius's order: know life and serve the living first

games.q: the question and the answer — tap the pairs.
p: the student who asks about death
care in the rites, remember parents

s: Confucius tells Zilu that death is a foolish thing to ask about
he never calls the question foolish. he puts it in order: life first.
Zilu asks about serving spirits before he asks about death
both answers point him back to the living first.
the Analects show no care for funerals or the dead
they speak of care in the rites and remembering parents long after.

games.q: you're Confucius. your blunt student Zilu asks: may I ask about death? what do you say?
o: here is exactly what happens after we die.
not yet knowing life, how can you know death?
games.why: he answers with a question that sets an order: life first. readers still argue whether it's wisdom or a gentle sidestep.

practice: Notice what's actually around you, the light in the room, a sound outside, the chair holding you up, and bring to mind one living person who's part of your day.
What does today ask of you, for them: a call, a meal, a little patience? If death comes to mind, let it, and then gently come back to today.

wordCard.voice: First: Confucius's order of things. Serve the living before the spirits, know life before death. Today's word.

orig.say: way jir SHUNG, yen jir SUH
orig.note: Classical Chinese, Analects 11.11: not yet knowing life, how know death. Modern Mandarin reading.

carryVoice: Your line: the kitchen table. Life first, and the rest in its order. Day seven hundred eighty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Analects 1.9 (Zengzi on funeral rites and remembering)
